episode_thesis: Rob Carver argues that trend following earns most of its return (about 70%) from trending asset-class indices and the rest from relative trends, that position sizing should follow Kelly logic tempered by Sharpe uncertainty (so no static, concentration-prone sizing), and that trend works best in bonds because forecasters expect rates to mean-revert while equity analysts extrapolate. He also argues that no hidden edge exists beyond marginal gains and error avoidance, and that neither market timing ('missing the best days') nor timing the trend strategy itself holds up. Niels adds the June 2025 drawdown context, shipping-data macro signals, and the case for staying invested through flat spells.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following is positively skewed at the right time frequency; in Sharpe units a good year is about +2 and a bad year about -1, so a drawdown is best read as a multiple of annual volatility.
worldview_premises.support: Own rule of thumb from live and backtest results (current drawdown -1.3 Sharpe units in 2025; long-run Sharpe 0.5-1).

worldview_premises.premise: Trend works where consensus expects mean reversion and is wrong; mean reversion works where consensus expects trends and is wrong.
worldview_premises.support: Ilmanen (AQR) paper on how bond investors are contrarian while equity investors extrapolate.

worldview_premises.premise: Under Gaussian returns, known Sharpe and unlimited leverage, CAGR is maximised by setting annualised volatility equal to the Sharpe ratio (Kelly); because the Sharpe is uncertain and skew matters, practical targets sit well below it.
worldview_premises.support: Pure maths ('you can't argue with it'); his own target is under half of Kelly.

worldview_premises.premise: Positive skew raises the optimal volatility target by less than people think, so it cannot easily be converted into higher returns.
A higher Sharpe gives a higher CAGR with leverage unless the Sharpe gain costs too much positive skew; fixed-stop, static sizing adds skew but loses too much Sharpe.
worldview_premises.support: Own research, consistent with Saratini and Quantica studies.

worldview_premises.premise: Letting winners run is partly anecdotal bias; at portfolio level it concentrates risk so a reversal causes big losses.
worldview_premises.support: Cocoa anecdote; the unnamed trend manager's 2025 loss.

worldview_premises.premise: Only the buy-or-not decision can be discretionary; sizing, holding period, stops and portfolio optimisation should be systematic, and systematic volatility forecasts are hard to beat.
worldview_premises.support: Own judgment and Marshall Wace's practice of feeding forecasts into an optimiser; he doubts his own discretionary skill.

worldview_premises.premise: There is no big undiscovered secret; manager differences come from marginal gains (beta cleaning, execution, cost-aware optimisation) and avoiding errors, and outcome differences are largely luck.
worldview_premises.support: Years in the industry; cycling 'marginal gains' analogy.

worldview_premises.premise: Capital adequacy rules can cause crises (Basel 2 contributed to 2008), so loosening bank rules or treating crypto as bank assets is risky.

Timing the market by missing days is absurd; avoiding the worst days beats missing the best days only because equity returns are negatively skewed, and random day-missing raises dispersion; the honest case for equities is the risk premium.
Timing the trend-following strategy itself would need meaningful autocorrelation of annual returns; measured on gross returns it is weak and fades at longer horizons.
worldview_premises.support: His own gross-return test, plus the Winton paper.

worldview_premises.premise: OTC liquidity can vanish suddenly, and IP leakage between CTAs is minor (staff moves bring a fresh perspective).
worldview_premises.support: His fixed-income experience in 2009; industry knowledge.

mechanism_chains.topic: Trend the asset-class index, then add relative trends

steps.to: Build an index weighted equally by volatility (US about 10% rather than 70%)
steps.why: Gives a usable asset-class factor where market cap has no meaning (copper)

steps.to: Apply that signal to every instrument in the class
steps.why: Equivalent to trading a metals or equity factor (all long or all short)

steps.to: Add market-neutral residual momentum versus the vol-normalised index over six months
steps.why: Residual trends at about one-month holding periods but mean-reverts at very short and very long horizons

steps.to: Results almost identical to plain trend following; about 70% of profit from the index and 30% from relative trends
steps.why: Decomposition of performance

steps.to: A limited-capital investor can trade the main instrument per class (S&P, 5-10y bond, gold) for about 70% of performance
steps.why: Main instrument carries the factor

mechanism_chains.evidence: His last book's tests; PCA exercise in crypto (70% Bitcoin) and the equity PCA matching cap weights; metals would likely show two factors (precious and industrial).
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Factor structure is unclear outside equities and crypto; a PCA of trend returns (replication) differs from a PCA of markets.

steps.from: Remove further components beyond the first
steps.to: A mean-reverting residual may remain
steps.why: Less intuitive components may be tradeable

steps.from: PCA across the whole futures universe
steps.to: Use it as a trading strategy, not only a risk tool
steps.why: Novel use he plans to write about

mechanism_chains.topic: Kelly sizing to a conservative volatility target

steps.to: Run annualised volatility equal to the Sharpe ratio (50% vol at Sharpe 0.5)
steps.why: Kelly under Gaussian returns, known Sharpe, infinite leverage

steps.from: Sharpe is uncertain and returns are skewed
steps.to: Negative skew needs a lower target, positive skew a higher one but only slightly
steps.why: Skew changes the optimum less than people assume

steps.to: Target well below Kelly (his is under half; most CTAs run lower)
steps.why: Nobody can forecast near-term Sharpe well enough to double the risk target

mechanism_chains.evidence: Theory plus his own estimate of a 0.5-1 Sharpe.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Assumptions break: non-Gaussian returns, unknown Sharpe, limited leverage.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why static, let-it-ride sizing loses at portfolio level

steps.to: Extra positive skew
steps.why: Hanging on to winners with one entry and one stop

steps.to: Higher dispersion and concentration
steps.why: Single-market anecdotes (cocoa) hide portfolio-level concentration

steps.to: Portfolio volatility far above target at peaks, so losses are large when the position reverses
steps.why: Over-risked relative to the Sharpe actually expected; one manager's volatility reached about 90%

steps.to: Implies expected Sharpe of 0.9 or more, about twice a realistic 0.5
steps.why: Rob's inference

mechanism_chains.evidence: Saratini and Quantica studies agree: sharpe loss outweighs skew gain; one named-by-implication manager's 2025 loss.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Some investors can size the fund down; for them the risk may be appropriate.

mechanism_chains.topic: Consensus extrapolation explains where trend works

steps.from: Forecasters assume rates return to normal (4% expected 2009-2020, down from 6% in 1999)
steps.to: Rates actually persist
steps.why: Forecasts always mean-revert, reality does not

steps.from: Equity analysts extrapolate good and bad times
steps.to: Momentum is already priced in or overpriced
steps.why: Emotional extrapolation; separate level optimism bias

steps.to: Trend works better in bonds than in equity indices, which suffer V-shaped reversals
steps.why: Bond mean-reversion expectations are wrong; equity momentum is priced

steps.to: Bond carry, secular decline in rates and rising equity valuations give momentum a tailwind, stronger in bonds
steps.why: Long-run trends

mechanism_chains.evidence: Ilmanen's forecast 'whisker' charts and analyst EPS data; trend performance by asset class.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: He admits other explanations (carry, secular drift) may do the work; unclear which dominates.

mechanism_chains.topic: Timing the strategy: why it fails

steps.to: Needs meaningful autocorrelation of annual returns
steps.why: Positive would mean add after good years, negative the reverse

steps.to: Net returns look more negatively autocorrelated
steps.why: Fees are paid only when doing well

steps.to: Weak positive annual autocorrelation that vanishes at longer horizons, too weak to exploit after costs
steps.why: Strategy timing is as hard as market timing

mechanism_chains.evidence: His own test on gross momentum returns; Winton paper.

decision_process.practice: Convert every signal to a forecast on a -20 to +20 scale (10 = average bullish); trend signal on a volatility-equal-weighted asset-class index applied to all instruments, plus residual (relative) momentum over six months.
decision_process.why: A single numeric scale lets signals, including discretionary ones, be combined and tested.

decision_process.practice: Reduce position size when volatility rises during a trade and scale position with forecast strength (continuous, not discrete pyramiding); target volatility under half of Kelly.
decision_process.why: Backtests and the Saratini and Quantica studies favour both adjustments, with forecast scaling having the larger effect; protects against concentration.

decision_process.practice: Weighted average of systematic and discretionary forecasts (e.g. 50/50 or 70/30), with the weight set by testing the discretionary forecasts as a backtest; Black-Litterman is the heavier alternative.
Avoid discretionary views on volatility; keep sizing, holding period, stops and optimisation systematic.
decision_process.why: Systematic volatility forecasts are hard to beat.

decision_process.practice: Cost-aware portfolio optimisation across many illiquid markets; avoid trading too fast and over-concentrating.
decision_process.why: Separates profitable from less profitable managers; his own past mistakes.

decision_process.practice: Use simulations (random day-missing) and gross-return autocorrelation tests; test discretionary forecasts like a backtest.
decision_process.why: Extrapolates beyond one historical path and removes fee bias.

decision_process.practice: Express P&L as an annualised Sharpe ratio to judge a drawdown against long-run expectations.

speakers.evidence_style: Own backtests (since 1970) and live results, simulations, and published papers (Asness, Ilmanen, Saratini, Quantica, Winton, Black-Litterman); first-principles maths for Kelly; caveats of anecdotal bias; admits uncertainty and avoids naming managers.

disagreements.topic: Risk of static (unadjusted) sizing at a high-volatility manager

positions.speaker: Rob Carver
positions.position: Static sizing lets concentration push risk far above target and implies an over-optimistic Sharpe of about 0.9 or more.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Ledger fix applied: Saratini and Quantica find both vol-adjusting and forecast scaling help, with forecast scaling (pyramiding) the bigger effect; the original ledger text said differences were small.
Ledger fix applied: Niels says only that the manager's volatility reached about 90%; the Kelly inference of an expected Sharpe of 0.9 or more (about twice 0.5) is Rob's.
The long-run Sharpe of 0.5-1 and the 'one-in-10 to one-in-20 year' drawdown label are self-estimates with no data shown.
The 70/30 split between index and relative trends comes from Rob's own book and is not independently reproduced; the equity PCA statement is a guess ('would probably').

He says trend works in bonds because investors expect mean reversion, but also lists carry and secular rate declines as explanations and says he does not know which dominates; the behavioural story is not separated from the tailwind story.
Box and container data are claimed to have a strong predictive record, but only a newsletter source and survey readings are given.
Rob says positive skew raises the Kelly target only modestly but also says a Sharpe loss from static sizing outweighs skew; neither is quantified in the episode.
Rob calls the IP-leakage risk minor while acknowledging that less systematic and higher-frequency strategies depend more on secrets.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs the speakers treat as informative: strength of trend signals across asset classes (currently weak, so low risk); trend of the volatility-equal-weighted asset-class index as the main driver of trend returns; consensus forecasts for rates and equity earnings as contrarian input (forecasters assume mean reversion, so persistence favours bond trend); realised portfolio concentration and volatility relative to target; Bank of America box survey and container volumes as demand nowcasts; bank capital rules as a financial-stability risk. Horizon is months for trend and years for the Sharpe and Kelly arguments.
reader_inferences: (reader) Rob's 70/30 finding implies most trend-following alpha is a factor-timing bet at the asset-class level, which is why replicators and a few-factor view are plausible; his stated caution is that PCA of trend returns differs from PCA of markets.
(reader) His Kelly and concentration arguments together imply that skew-seeking sizing is a bet on an unusually high Sharpe, so sizing choices are really Sharpe-confidence choices.

(reader) The consensus-extrapolation story gives a testable prediction: trend should be weaker where forecasters extrapolate (equity indices) and stronger where they assume mean reversion (rates, possibly gold), which matches the post-2000 asset-class record he cites.
(reader) Niels's reading of shipping data as a demand warning and Rob's low-risk positioning point in the same direction (no strong trend, weakening activity) but are not connected by either speaker.
